questions.stem: Which statement best describes mental health?
options: A diagnosis given only to people who have fully recovered from a mental disorder
A fixed characteristic that a person is born with and cannot change
Wellbeing that lets a person cope with stress, work and contribute
The complete absence of any negative emotion such as sadness, anger or worry
questions.explanation: Mental health is more than the absence of a disorder: it includes emotional, psychological and social wellbeing and the ability to handle normal stresses. Feeling sad or worried at times is part of good mental health.

questions.stem: Two people have the same diagnosis of depression. One has supportive friends and stable work; the other is socially isolated and unemployed. Why might their mental health differ?
options: Social factors affect physical but not mental health
Sociocultural factors can protect or harm mental health
A diagnosis means mental health is identical in all people
Only biological factors affect a person's mental health
questions.explanation: Mental health is shaped by the interaction of biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Social support and meaningful work are protective, while isolation and unemployment are risk factors.

questions.stem: Which is a biological factor that can affect mental health?
options: a supportive group of close friends at school
experiencing racism in the community
a genetic vulnerability to a mental disorder
a pessimistic way of interpreting life events
questions.explanation: Genes, brain chemistry, sleep, diet and drug use are biological factors. Thinking styles are psychological, and friendships and racism are sociocultural.

questions.stem: Which is a psychological factor that can negatively affect mental health?
options: a habit of thinking the worst will always happen
a family history of anxiety disorders and depression
living in poverty with an insecure, low income
poor sleep caused by shift work
questions.explanation: Psychological factors involve thoughts, emotions and coping, such as catastrophic thinking or low self-esteem. Family history is biological, poverty is sociocultural, and sleep loss is biological.

questions.stem: Which list contains only sociocultural factors that can negatively affect mental health?
options: poverty, low serotonin levels and social isolation
harassment at work, poor diet and low self-esteem
social isolation, genetic risk and negative thinking
poverty, harassment at work and social isolation
questions.explanation: Poverty, harassment and isolation all come from a person's social and cultural environment. Serotonin, diet and genes are biological; low self-esteem and negative thinking are psychological.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to test whether regular exercise improves mood in adults with mild low mood. Which design allows a cause-and-effect conclusion?
options: randomly assigning participants to an exercise program or a control group
surveying people about how much they exercise and how they feel
observing people at a local gym and recording how happy they seem
interviewing a focus group about their views on exercise and mood
questions.explanation: Only an experiment, with the independent variable manipulated and random allocation, can show that exercise causes a change in mood. A survey could find a relationship but not establish its direction.

questions.stem: Why might an experiment testing the effect of alcohol on mental health raise more ethical concerns than a survey of drinking habits?
options: Surveys never need informed consent from the people who take part
Experiments cannot have their participants' results kept confidential
Surveys always involve deceiving participants about the aim
Participants would be exposed to a substance that could harm them
questions.explanation: In an experiment the researcher deliberately gives a potentially harmful condition, so the risk to wellbeing is greater. A survey records existing behaviour, though it still needs consent and confidentiality.

questions.stem: How could the media positively influence mental health?
options: By showing people with mental illness mainly as violent and unpredictable
By avoiding any mention of mental health to prevent people worrying
By presenting mental illness as a sign of personal weakness
By portraying people with mental illness accurately and showing recovery
questions.explanation: Accurate and hopeful portrayals reduce stigma and encourage people to seek help. Portraying people as violent or weak reinforces stigma and discourages help-seeking.

questions.stem: Which change to employment conditions is most likely to improve employees' mental health?
options: reducing excessive workloads and acting quickly on harassment
increasing workloads so that employees have less time to worry
removing breaks so that tasks are completed sooner each day
discouraging staff from talking about stress with managers
questions.explanation: Heavy workloads, harassment and noise are negative sociocultural factors in workplaces, while manageable demands, support and respectful treatment protect mental health.

questions.stem: How do the ethical issues in experimental research on mental health typically differ from those in non-experimental research?
options: Experiments do not need consent because participants are randomly allocated
Non-experimental research always requires deceiving participants about the aim
Experiments impose a condition, so any risk of harm must be justified
Non-experimental research never involves any risk to privacy or confidentiality
questions.explanation: In an experiment the researcher deliberately exposes participants to a condition, such as sleep loss, which may harm them or withhold a benefit. Non-experimental research measures existing behaviour, though consent, privacy and confidentiality still apply.

questions.stem: Which is a positive sociocultural factor for mental health?
options: a genetic tendency towards calmness
an optimistic style of thinking about events
getting enough sleep on most nights
friendships and regular leisure activities
questions.explanation: Friendships, leisure, education and good working environments come from the social and cultural environment. Genetic temperament and sleep are biological; optimism is psychological.

questions.stem: What is meant by the statement 'Definitions of mental disorders are culturally constructed'?
options: All cultures define and recognise every mental disorder in exactly the same way
Mental disorders are defined only by biological tests carried out in a laboratory
What counts as a disorder depends on a culture's norms, values and time period
Mental disorders are invented and do not cause real distress to anyone
questions.explanation: Judgements about what is abnormal depend on cultural expectations, which differ between places and change over time. This does not mean distress is not real.

questions.stem: Homosexuality was listed as a mental disorder in early editions of the DSM and was removed in the 1970s. What does this change best show?
options: The DSM has listed the same disorders in every edition since it began
Sexual orientation is now classed as a personality disorder
Cultural attitudes have no influence on how disorders are defined
Definitions change as social attitudes and evidence change
questions.explanation: The removal followed changing social attitudes, activism and research showing that homosexuality is not associated with impaired functioning. It is a clear example of how classification reflects the culture of its time.

questions.stem: A behaviour such as hearing the voice of a deceased relative may be accepted as normal in one cultural group but seen as a symptom in another. What is the main implication for diagnosis?
options: Clinicians should apply one culture's norms to every patient equally
Behaviours accepted in one culture can never indicate a disorder
Diagnosis should be based only on the number of symptoms reported
Clinicians must interpret symptoms within the person's cultural context
questions.explanation: The same experience can have different meanings in different cultures, so judging it against the clinician's own norms risks misdiagnosis. Context matters, though cultural acceptance does not rule out a disorder in every case.

questions.stem: How can experiencing racism affect the mental health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people?
options: It is a chronic stressor linked to anxiety, depression and psychological distress
It affects physical health only and has no link with psychological wellbeing
It strengthens mental health by building resilience in every person who experiences it
It affects people only when the racism is physically violent
questions.explanation: Repeated experiences of racism, including everyday and systemic racism, act as ongoing stressors and are linked to anxiety, depression and distress. Racism also adds to the effects of intergenerational trauma.

questions.stem: Refugees who experience racism after arriving in Australia may have poorer mental health. Which explanation fits a biopsychosocial view?
options: Mental health depends only on what happened to them before arrival in Australia
Racism affects refugee children but not adults who arrive as refugees
Racism adds social stress to previous trauma and can reduce a sense of belonging
Racism only affects refugees who do not speak English at home
questions.explanation: Many refugees have already experienced trauma and loss. Racism adds ongoing stress, isolation and barriers to work and services, which can worsen mental health.

questions.stem: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, which factor is widely recognised as central to social and emotional wellbeing?
options: replacing traditional practices with Western ones
connection to Country, culture, family and community
individual achievement measured by income and status
living away from family to develop independence
questions.explanation: Social and emotional wellbeing for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples is a holistic concept that includes connection to Country, culture, spirituality, family and community. Disruption of these connections harms wellbeing.

questions.stem: A clinician from a different cultural background interprets a patient's avoidance of eye contact as a sign of depression, when in the patient's culture it shows respect. This illustrates:
options: a problem that only occurs with patients who speak English
misdiagnosis caused by cultural differences between clinician and patient
an accurate diagnosis based on a culture-free symptom checklist
the patient deliberately hiding their real symptoms from the clinician
questions.explanation: When clinician and patient come from different cultures, behaviour can be misread, leading to misdiagnosis or inappropriate treatment. Understanding the patient's cultural norms helps prevent this.

questions.stem: Which is a likely problem when a clinician and patient do not share a language?
options: The patient will always receive a faster and more accurate diagnosis
The clinician will no longer need to gain informed consent
The patient's cultural background becomes irrelevant to care
Symptoms may be misunderstood and trust may be harder to build
questions.explanation: Language barriers make it harder to describe feelings accurately and to build rapport. Trained interpreters and culturally responsive practice can help reduce these problems.

questions.stem: DSM-5 places emphasis on cultural sensitivity. Which feature reflects this?
options: a structured interview to explore how culture shapes a person's problem
a requirement that all patients be assessed in English only
a rule that cultural beliefs must be ignored to keep diagnosis objective
a single list of symptoms that applies identically in every culture
questions.explanation: DSM-5 includes the Cultural Formulation Interview, a set of questions that helps clinicians understand how a person's cultural background affects their experience, explanation and help-seeking.

questions.stem: Why might people from some cultural groups be less likely to seek help from mainstream mental health services?
options: Mental disorders do not occur in people from other cultural groups
Mainstream services refuse to treat anyone who was born outside Australia
People from other cultures always prefer medication to talking therapy
Services may not reflect their beliefs about illness and may carry stigma
questions.explanation: Help-seeking is affected by cultural beliefs about the causes of distress, stigma within the community, language barriers and past negative experiences with services. Culturally safe services can improve access.

questions.stem: Which DSM edition introduced the Cultural Formulation Interview to support culturally sensitive assessment?
options: DSM-IV
DSM-5
DSM-II
DSM-III
questions.explanation: DSM-5 includes the Cultural Formulation Interview, a set of questions about how a person understands their problem in cultural terms, the supports they have and their expectations of help.

questions.stem: Which is a positive influence social media can have on mental health?
options: disrupting sleep through late-night scrolling
connecting isolated people with supportive communities
encouraging constant comparison with others' highlights
exposing young people to cyberbullying and harassment
questions.explanation: Social media can reduce isolation, provide peer support and give access to mental health information and services. Comparison, cyberbullying and sleep disruption are negative influences.

questions.stem: A teenager feels worse about herself after scrolling through friends' holiday photos. Which explanation is most likely?
options: the norm of reciprocity when liking other people's posts
stimulus discrimination between real and edited photos
upward social comparison with carefully selected images
downward social comparison with less fortunate people
questions.explanation: Comparing oneself with others who seem better off, especially using edited highlights, can lower mood and self-esteem. Downward comparison, with those worse off, tends to make people feel better.

questions.stem: Mental health organisations such as Beyond Blue and Lifeline use social media. What is the main benefit?
options: It guarantees that all information shared is accurate
It removes privacy risks from discussing mental health
It reaches people who might not otherwise seek help
It replaces the need for any trained counsellors
questions.explanation: Social media can share information, reduce stigma and point people to support. To be effective and safe it needs trained staff, moderation and accurate content.

questions.stem: A study finds that teenagers who spend more time on social media report more symptoms of depression. Which conclusion is justified?
options: There is no link, because correlational studies show nothing at all
There is a relationship, but social media use may not be the cause
Social media use causes depression in all teenagers who use it
Depression causes all teenagers to use much more social media
questions.explanation: A correlation shows the two variables are related, but not which causes which. Depressed teens may use social media more, or a third variable such as poor sleep may affect both.

questions.stem: A student wants to reduce her social media use. She earns an hour of a favourite activity for every day she stays under 30 minutes. Which technique is she using?
options: cognitive restructuring of unhelpful beliefs
behaviour modification using positive reinforcement
behaviour modification using aversive punishment
systematic desensitisation using a fear hierarchy
questions.explanation: Behaviour modification applies operant conditioning to change behaviour. Earning a pleasant reward for the target behaviour is positive reinforcement.

questions.stem: Which is the best first step in a behaviour-modification program to reduce social media use?
options: punishing all social media use from the first day
asking friends to post more often to increase motivation
recording a baseline of current use to measure change against
deleting every account permanently without any planning
questions.explanation: A baseline shows how much the behaviour occurs before the program, so progress can be measured. Clear, specific goals and consequences are then set.

questions.stem: A person sets their phone to block social media apps after 9 pm and loses a dollar to a savings jar each time they override it. Losing the dollar is an example of:
options: response cost
positive reinforcement
negative reinforcement
aversive punishment
questions.explanation: Response cost removes something valued after an unwanted behaviour to reduce it. Aversive punishment would add an unpleasant stimulus instead.

questions.stem: A school plans to use a behaviour-modification program to reduce students' social media use without telling them. What is the main ethical concern?
options: Students would be unable to use any technology during the program
Students have not consented to having their behaviour changed
Behaviour modification never changes the behaviour of adolescents
Reinforcement is unethical in every program used with young people
questions.explanation: Changing someone's behaviour without their knowledge or consent breaches respect for their autonomy. Programs should be voluntary, transparent and focused on the person's own goals.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a chemical addiction and a behavioural addiction?
options: A chemical addiction is always mild; a behavioural one is always severe
A chemical addiction affects the brain; a behavioural one affects only habits
A chemical addiction involves a substance; a behavioural one involves an activity
A chemical addiction involves an activity; a behavioural one involves a substance
questions.explanation: Chemical addictions involve dependence on a substance such as alcohol or nicotine; behavioural addictions involve compulsive engagement in an activity such as gambling. Both involve the brain's reward system.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument that excessive social media use could be considered an addiction?
options: Social media apps are free to download and easy to access
People often use social media while doing other activities
It can continue despite harm and activates reward pathways
Most people enjoy using social media and use it every day
questions.explanation: Addiction involves compulsive use, loss of control and continuing despite negative consequences, linked to the brain's reward system. Frequent, enjoyable use alone is not evidence of addiction.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument against classifying excessive social media use as an addiction?
options: Only substances such as drugs can affect the brain's reward pathways at all
Behavioural addictions such as gambling are not recognised anywhere
It could pathologise ordinary behaviour, and agreed diagnostic criteria are lacking
Social media use is never linked to any harm in any person who uses it
questions.explanation: Critics argue that labelling heavy use as an addiction risks treating common behaviour as a disorder, and that there are no agreed criteria for social media addiction. Gambling disorder, by contrast, is recognised in DSM-5.

questions.stem: Why do social media notifications and likes keep people checking their phones so often?
options: They are punishers, so people check to make them stop
They are unconditioned stimuli that cause reflex responses
They are delivered on a variable schedule, which produces persistent checking
They are delivered on a fixed schedule, so people know exactly when to check
questions.explanation: Likes and messages arrive unpredictably, like a variable reinforcement schedule, which produces high and persistent rates of responding. This is one reason social media use can become compulsive.

questions.stem: At what point is social media use most likely to be considered problematic?
options: When it interferes with sleep, study, relationships or wellbeing
When a person uses more than one app on the same day
When a person uses it to keep in touch with family overseas
When a person posts photos of their weekend activities
questions.explanation: Use becomes a concern when it causes harm or impairment, such as lost sleep, falling grades or conflict, and when the person struggles to cut back. The amount of time alone is not the only measure.

questions.stem: A psychologist gives mental health advice to a large audience on a public social media account. What is the main ethical risk?
options: The psychologist will always breach a follower's confidentiality
Public advice is illegal for all registered health professionals in Australia
Followers cannot understand any advice unless it is very technical
Advice cannot be tailored, and followers may treat it as personal treatment
questions.explanation: General advice can help, but without assessment it may not suit an individual and may delay proper treatment. Psychologists must also take care with accuracy and boundaries in public forums.
